title: 9 Best Hotel Phone Systems in 2026
summary: Nine hotel phone systems compared for 2026: RingCentral, Dialpad, Aircall, Quo, Smith.ai, Goodcall, Akia, HelloShift and Conduit, with published pricing.
body_markdown:
*Written by Punn Kam, ex-Google AI engineer and Y Combinator repeat founder. He is the co-founder of Conduit, an AI agent platform built for hospitality, serving 300+ hospitality brands in 140+ languages. Last updated August 26, 2026.*


A hotel phone system in 2026 is two purchases, not one. There is the telephony layer that carries the call, and there is the agent that answers it. The mainstream business phone systems now all ship an autonomous voice agent, so the question is no longer whether AI answers. It is whether the thing answering can see a reservation.


## What should a hotel phone system do in 2026?


Five things, in rough order of how often they decide the purchase.


- Answer every call, including after hours, without sending guests to voicemail.
- Know who is calling, which means matching the number to a reservation rather than a contact card.
- Complete the request. Moving a checkout, adding a night, reissuing a door code, taking a payment.
- Hand off cleanly, with context, when a person is genuinely needed.
- Keep the phone and the messaging thread in one history, so a guest who calls and then texts is not starting over.


Points one, four, and five are solved by several products now. Points two and three are where the field splits, and they are the ones worth testing.


## Do generic business phone systems work for hotels?


They work as telephony, and their AI answers questions rather than acting on bookings.


All the major platforms now ship an autonomous agent. RingCentral has AI Receptionist at $39 a month as an add-on or $49 standalone, trained on your website, FAQs, and uploaded documents. Aircall has AI Voice Agents that handle frequent questions and transfer with context. Dialpad has Dialpad AI Agent, described as autonomous across voice and digital. Quo, formerly OpenPhone, has Sona answering 24/7 from $19 per user.


That is real capability, and it is trained on documents rather than connected to your PMS. The practical consequence: the agent will tell a guest that checkout is 11am, and it will not move that guest's checkout to 2pm. One of those is an answer. The other is the job.


The second mismatch is the unit. These products price per user, per seat, or per licence, because they were built for teams where staff count drives cost. A hotel's cost driver is rooms and occupancy. Aircall requires three licences minimum and twenty-five on its Custom plan, which is a strange shape for a property with two people on the desk.

Two things stand out. The hospitality-specific tools mostly do not publish pricing, while the telephony products almost all do. And the telephony products are, on the whole, cheaper, because answering a question is a smaller job than completing a request.


## Which one should a hotel actually buy?


It depends on what your calls are made of, so audit that before shortlisting anything.


If most inbound calls are new bookings and directions, a telephony product with an AI receptionist is genuinely sufficient and much cheaper. RingCentral at $39 or Quo at $19 a user will cover it, and paying for a hospitality platform would be waste.


If a meaningful share of calls are from guests who already have a reservation, the calculation inverts. Every one of those calls that ends in "let me take a message" is a call you paid to answer and still have to handle. That is the case the hospitality tools exist for, and the question to put to each vendor is not whether the agent is smart but what it is allowed to change.


If your operation is a single property with a front desk that is staffed most of the day, the honest answer is that you may not need any of this yet, and the after-hours window is the only gap worth pricing.


Our position, stated plainly: Conduit is in the third row of that table for a reason. It prices per unit from $18 a month rather than per seat, runs voice and text on one agent so the call and the thread share a history, and writes back to the PMS rather than only reading it. Our published automation band is 70-90% across the platform, and Cash Flow Street, a 35-property manager, runs at 96%. Watch-out: if your callers are not guests with bookings, none of that is worth the premium over a $19 seat.

## FAQ


### What is the best phone system for a hotel in 2026?


It depends on whether your callers already have reservations. For booking and information calls, a business phone system with an AI receptionist such as RingCentral or Quo is enough. For in-stay guest calls, you need an agent connected to your PMS.


### Can RingCentral or Dialpad work as a hotel phone system?


Yes as telephony. Both now ship autonomous AI agents, but neither publishes a property management integration, so the agent can answer questions and cannot change a booking.


### How much does an AI phone answering service cost for a hotel?


The published range is wide. RingCentral's AI Receptionist is $39 or $49 a month, Quo starts at $19 per user, Goodcall at $79 per agent, Smith.ai at $300 for 30 calls, and Conduit at $18 per unit per month. Most hospitality-specific vendors do not publish rates at all.


### Do hotels still need a PBX?


Most independents no longer run on-premise hardware, and the in-room phone is a smaller part of the job than the inbound line. Prioritise the inbound guest call, since that is where bookings and complaints arrive.


### What is the difference between an AI receptionist and a hospitality AI agent?


An AI receptionist answers from a knowledge base of documents and routes the call. A hospitality agent is connected to the reservation system, so it can look up a specific stay and change it. The gap shows up the first time a guest asks for something rather than asking about something.
